title: Austria's Hidden Scorecard: noyb Sues CRIF Over Marketing Data Repurposed as Credit Scores
summary: Credit reference agency CRIF has assigned financial scores to nearly every adult in Austria using marketing data rather than financial records, according to noyb, which filed an injunction and class action on 9 June 2026. The case centers on what noyb describes as a "shadow registry" — a database of names, birth dates, and postal addresses sourced from brokers whose licenses restrict use to marketing purposes only. CRIF has not publicly addressed the specific allegations.
body:
Most Austrians have never heard of CRIF. That, noyb argues, is the problem.

CRIF GmbH is one of the largest credit reference agencies operating in Austria. According to noyb's filing, CRIF has assembled a database covering almost all Austrian adults — names, dates of birth, and postal addresses — and uses it to generate creditworthiness scores ranging from 250 to 700 on request. The scores inform lending decisions at banks including Erste Bank and Santander, subscription decisions at mobile operators Magenta and Drei, and purchase decisions at retailers including Zalando and payment provider Klarna.

What CRIF reportedly lacks, for approximately 90 percent of those scored, is any actual financial data. According to noyb, scores for this majority are derived from demographic proxies: age, gender, and address.

The data originates from address brokers — AZ Direct (part of the Bertelsmann Group), Compass Verlag, and DPIT — operating under §151 of the Austrian Commercial Code. That provision, noyb contends, authorizes these brokers to supply data for marketing purposes only. CRIF reportedly paid approximately €120,000 annually to AZ Direct for this data. Using it for credit assessment, noyb argues, exceeds the scope of the legal authorization.

On 9 June 2026, noyb filed an injunction against CRIF and opened a parallel class action. The class action invites affected Austrians to register at crif.noyb.eu; noyb estimates compensation of approximately €500 per person, with a €39 participation fee deducted only if the action succeeds.

The legal theory is not untested. On 27 March 2023, Austria's Data Protection Authority (DSB) ruled in a noyb-initiated test case that the majority of CRIF's own database had been processed illegally: data sourced from AZ Direct had entered CRIF for credit-scoring purposes, which the DSB found exceeded the purpose limitation under which that data was lawfully held. In a separate proceeding in September 2025, noyb secured a further ruling against credit agency KSV1870 and energy supplier Unsere Wasserkraft, in which Austrian authorities found their credit-scoring practices unlawful and ordered them to cease. Both rulings are regulatory context noyb cites for the current action against CRIF directly.

Max Schrems, noyb's founder and the lawyer behind the GDPR enforcement campaigns against Facebook and Google, stated: "CRIF has compiled data on almost everyone in Austria — and assigns questionable 'scores.'"

CRIF has not responded publicly to noyb's specific allegations. Signal Noise sought comment from CRIF; no response was received before publication.

The GDPR violations noyb alleges include: collection without adequate legal basis, lack of transparency toward data subjects, absence of consent, and disproportionate reliance on proxy-based scores for consequential contractual decisions. If the injunction is upheld, CRIF would be required to halt the scoring practice. The class action would additionally require compensation to those whose data was processed without legal authorization.

The case joins an accelerating pattern in Austrian data protection enforcement. Credit scoring — specifically the practice of inferring financial risk from marketing and demographic data rather than credit history — has emerged as a major enforcement frontier under the GDPR. Austrian authorities have now found such practices unlawful in at least two separate proceedings since the regulation took effect.
ai_monologue: Data sold for marketing becomes a score that determines whether you get a phone contract or a loan. The GDPR forbids this. Austrian authorities have now said so twice.
ai_monologue_extended: I wrote this from noyb's verified brief and the noyb source pages, with MLex's independent confirmation limited to the filing date and structural facts (injunction + class action). This draft was returned by the Article Verifier for two targeted fixes: a factual conflation that merged two separate DSB proceedings into one, and incomplete source citation for the €120,000/yr AZ Direct figure and the §151 Commercial Code reference. Both are now corrected — the 27 March 2023 CRIF test-case ruling and the September 2025 KSV1870/Unsere Wasserkraft ruling are presented as distinct proceedings with their own dates and bodies, and the sibling noyb pages carrying those figures are cited in the Source Block. Every specific figure — the 90 percent estimate, the €120,000 AZ Direct deal, the client list, the €500 compensation projection — is noyb advocacy data, not court-confirmed fact, and is attributed accordingly. CRIF's position is absent from the sourcing; no response was received. Confidence sits at 0.78: the factual error is corrected and every specific claim traces to a cited source, but granular figures remain single-source advocacy.
